final_candidates.decision_summary: Near-maximal pathogenicity proxy together with strong evolutionary and sequence-model intolerance supports severe loss of function.
Charge reversal at this strongly intolerant position has a very high LOF-proxy score and is likely to disrupt enzyme function.
The charge-reversing substitution combines a high pathogenicity prediction with strong evolutionary and sequence-model intolerance.

stop_reason.detail: Additional available evidence is non-applicable, redundant, or unrelated to MTHFR loss of function and is unlikely to change the Top-3.

history.rationale: Charge reversal at a conserved catalytic-domain arginine is likely to strongly disrupt substrate or cofactor interactions while retaining a full-length protein.

R157E combines a high pathogenicity prediction with evolutionary rarity and extreme sequence-model implausibility. The charge reversal is likely disruptive, although its predicted pathogenicity is slightly below that of W95D and D159K.
The high LOF-proxy score and strong intolerance signals support retaining R157E in the Top-3. No candidate-specific annotation was available to change that conclusion.
Reversing the charge of this catalytic-domain acidic residue should disrupt local active-site geometry and electrostatics.

The high pathogenicity score and strong sequence implausibility support a damaging effect from this charge reversal. Low mutant frequency provides additional, though lower-reliability, evidence of intolerance.
Its strong LOF-proxy prediction and poor evolutionary and sequence plausibility continue to support severe functional disruption. The annotation result is non-informative.
Replacing a bulky aromatic residue near the catalytic-domain core with an acidic residue is expected to severely impair catalytic-domain structure or cofactor binding.

W95D has the strongest pathogenicity prediction and is highly disfavored by both evolutionary and sequence-model priors, a combination consistent with severe disruption. Its location in the catalytic domain and radical aromatic-to-acidic change make it the leading LOF candidate.

The near-maximal LOF-proxy score, evolutionary rarity, and sequence implausibility remain strongly supportive. The generic annotation fallback supplies no position-specific reason to alter its leading rank.
Introducing proline at this catalytic-domain arginine should remove its positive charge and perturb the surrounding secondary structure.
The low pathogenicity prediction and high sequence-model plausibility both argue against strong LOF. Absence of proline in the shallow homolog alignment is insufficient to overcome those signals.

rejection.reason: The low pathogenicity prediction and high sequence-model plausibility both argue against strong LOF. Absence of proline in the shallow homolog alignment is insufficient to overcome those signals.

history.rationale: An aromatic-to-acidic substitution in the conserved catalytic region is likely to disrupt packing and ligand-associated interactions.

Although the substitution is evolutionarily rare and sequence-implausible, its pathogenicity score is only moderate. It is therefore less compelling than four alternatives with substantially stronger LOF-proxy evidence.

rejection.reason: Although the substitution is evolutionarily rare and sequence-implausible, its pathogenicity score is only moderate. It is therefore less compelling than four alternatives with substantially stronger LOF-proxy evidence.

history.rationale: The large charge and steric change at this catalytic-domain cysteine is likely to damage the local active-site fold.

C130R remains a strong backup because it is predicted pathogenic, absent among aligned homologs, and strongly sequence-implausible. It ranks below the leading three because its pathogenicity score and MSA coverage are modestly weaker.

C130R remains a credible backup because it combines a high LOF-proxy score with complete or near-complete intolerance in the evolutionary and sequence models. It remains below R157E because its phenotype score is modestly weaker.
